questions.prompt: What does a contract test check?
options: That a provider and a consumer agree on the requests and responses they exchange
That the UI looks correct
The provider's full business logic
The response time under load
questions.explanation: Contract tests verify the shape of the interaction both sides depend on, without a full end-to-end environment. Business logic and performance need other tests.

questions.prompt: In Pact, what does the provider do with the consumer's pact file?
options: Replays the recorded requests against the real provider and checks the responses match
Generates a UI from it
Deploys it to production
Ignores it unless the build fails
questions.explanation: Provider verification replays each interaction (with provider states set up) and compares real responses to the consumer's expectations.

questions.prompt: A consumer contract should include only the fields the consumer actually uses, not every field the provider returns.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Over-specified contracts break on harmless provider changes. Consumer-driven contracts express real needs, which gives providers freedom to change everything else.

questions.prompt: The provider wants to remove field `legacyCode`. How can they know whether it is safe?
options: Check whether any consumer's verified contract uses `legacyCode` (for example via a Pact Broker's can-i-deploy)
Remove it and watch for incidents
Ask only the newest consumer
Read the provider's unit tests
questions.explanation: Contracts document which consumers depend on which fields. A broker can answer whether a version is compatible with what is deployed. Guessing or asking one team misses other consumers.

questions.prompt: What is a provider state in Pact?
options: A named precondition (e.g. "order 42 exists") the provider sets up before replaying an interaction
The provider's HTTP status
The version of the provider
The provider's database password
questions.explanation: Provider states let an interaction be verified with the right data present, without the consumer knowing how the provider stores it.

questions.prompt: Which matchers make a consumer contract robust? Select all that apply.
options: Type matching for an id (any string), rather than a fixed value
A regex for a date format
"Each like" for arrays with at least one element
Exact match on a server-generated timestamp
questions.explanation: Matchers express the rule the consumer needs, not a sample value. Exact matching on a generated timestamp would fail on every real run.

questions.prompt: Consumer tests pass, provider verification passes, yet production breaks: the provider returns `price` as a string "9.99" in one rare branch. What is the most likely gap?
options: The contract only covered the common interaction; add an interaction (and provider state) for the rare branch
Contract testing cannot catch type changes
The consumer should parse everything as strings
Pact files are not versioned
questions.explanation: Contracts verify only the interactions they contain. Type matchers would catch the string if that branch were part of the contract.

questions.prompt: A team runs a full end-to-end environment of 14 services for every pull request just to check API compatibility, and it is slow and flaky. What would you propose?
options: Consumer-driven contract tests per pair, verified in each service's pipeline, plus a small number of end-to-end smoke tests
More retries in the end-to-end suite
Delete all integration testing
Test only in production
questions.explanation: Contracts move compatibility checks to fast, isolated builds. A thin end-to-end layer still checks wiring and configuration.

coding.title: Detect breaking changes against a consumer contract
coding.prompt:
A consumer contract is a dict of field name -> expected type name (`'str'`, `'int'`, `'float'`, `'bool'`, `'list'`, `'dict'`). Write `breaking(contract, response)` returning a sorted list of messages: `'<field>: missing'` when absent, `'<field>: expected <type>'` when present with the wrong type. Extra fields in the response are fine. `bool` must not count as `int`.

Example: `breaking({'id': 'str', 'total': 'float'}, {'id': 'a', 'total': '9.99', 'x': 1})` returns `['total: expected float']`.
coding.explanation: This is the heart of consumer-driven contracts: check only what the consumer needs, tolerate additions, and flag removals and type changes, the two changes that actually break clients.
hints: Map type names to Python types with a dict.
Skip fields that are not in the contract.

tests.name: Missing fields and bool vs int
tests.code:
r = breaking({'a': 'int', 'b': 'list', 'c': 'str'}, {'a': True, 'b': []})
assert r == ['a: expected int', 'c: missing'], r
